notes: No school, computing or course documents found (course layer deferred); four university-layer pages coded. Reconciled from coders A and B; repeated template sentences in the example-policies page are coded once.

documents.unit: AI at CWRU (AI Governance Committee, AI Task Force)
documents.title: Governance & Policies | AI at CWRU
documents.summary: The university AI governance page grounds AI use in existing integrity, security and privacy policies, requires approved tools and protection of restricted data, and leaves the decision on classroom AI to faculty.
documents.stance_why: The page says "Faculty retain discretion over whether and how to incorporate AI into their teaching and research" and sets no default for students, only data and accountability rules, so it delegates.

units.why: The page opens its policy section with "CWRU supports the responsible and innovative use of AI", an institution-wide statement of purpose, so it is a framework principle (P56) with an encouraging unit stance, addressed to all.
units.anchor: CWRU supports the responsible and innovative use of AI
units.frag_end: teaching, learning, research and university operations
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P56/general/informs; A gave unit_stance encourage, B permit. The sentence says CWRU 'supports the responsible and innovative use of AI', which welcomes AI, so encourage.

units.why: "including generative and agentic AI systems" sets what kind of AI the policy covers, a scope definition (P61), not a rule.
units.anchor: including generative and agentic AI systems
units.policy: CWRU's support for the responsible and innovative use of AI covers generative and agentic AI systems.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this phrase. The source says 'including generative and agentic AI systems', which sets the scope of the policy (P61), so it is kept; the anchor alone is a fragment, so a normalized statement is written.

units.why: "Rather than establishing AI policies in isolation, CWRU builds upon existing institutional requirements" states the framework approach: AI is governed through existing integrity, security and privacy rules. This is institution-level framing (P56), not a student rule.
units.anchor: Rather than establishing AI policies in isolation

units.why: "must use AI with integrity, transparency and accountability in accordance with applicable university policies" binds everyone and conditions AI use on existing policies; this is the general framework rule (P56), AI is permitted with conditions.
units.anchor: must use AI with integrity, transparency and accountability
units.frag_start: All members of the university community
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P56/must; A gave unit_stance neutral, B permit. 'must use AI with integrity, transparency and accountability' conditions AI use rather than banning it, so permit.

units.why: "Users remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity and appropriate use of AI-assisted work" makes users answerable for what they produce with AI, so P29 fits better than P31 because it is about responsibility, not only verification.
units.anchor: Users remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity and appropriate use of AI-assisted work.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P29/must; A gave unit_stance require, B permit. 'Users remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity and appropriate use of AI-assisted work' presupposes allowed AI use with accountability; nothing requires AI, so permit.

units.why: "Faculty retain discretion over whether and how to incorporate AI into their teaching and research" hands the decision to instructors (P04), set before the course; modality may because it grants discretion.
units.anchor: Faculty retain discretion over whether and how to incorporate AI

units.why: "Use university-approved AI tools" is a requirement under "you must follow these guidelines" and points users to vetted tools (P50), not a course-specific tool (P17).
units.anchor: Use university-approved AI tools.

units.why: "Avoid personal or unapproved consumer AI accounts, which may not provide the same data privacy and security protections" discourages unvetted tools for privacy reasons (P50); "Avoid" gives should-not.
units.anchor: Avoid personal or unapproved consumer AI accounts
units.frag_end: provide the same data privacy and security protections.

units.why: "Do not enter restricted university data... into any AI tool" is a flat ban on entering sensitive data, a data-protection rule (P50), not about assignments (so not P20).
units.anchor: Do not enter restricted university data

units.why: "Review applicable data security guidelines and research requirements before uploading documents" asks users to check rules before sharing data with AI; data protection (P50).
units.anchor: Review applicable data security guidelines and research requirements before uploading documents
units.frag_end: connecting AI tools to university systems.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P50/should; A gave unit_stance neutral, B restrict. 'Review applicable data security guidelines ... before uploading' is a procedural check that neither bans nor limits AI, so neutral.

units.why: The governance structure (AI Governance Committee, AI Strategy Committee, AI Task Force, working groups) says who oversees AI institutionally; it is a framework/oversight fact (P56) with no rule for use.
units.anchor: the AI Governance Committee and the AI Strategy Committee provide strategic direction and institutional oversight

units.why: "Use this form to report potential risks or inappropriate AI use" creates a reporting channel for AI concerns. It is not classification as misconduct (P36) or a student response right (P64), so no existing type fits.
units.anchor: Use this form to report potential risks or inappropriate AI use.
units.uncovered_note: A channel for anyone to report AI security, privacy or misuse concerns to the university.

documents.title: Guidance on integrating AI (artificial intelligence) into the CWRU classroom
documents.stance_why: The provost letter says "Faculty members have complete discretion" and lists a range from prohibition to open use with citation, so no single stance is set; it delegates.
documents.summary: A 2023 letter from the interim provost giving faculty complete discretion to prohibit, require permission for, or allow AI, asks them to state expectations in syllabi and enforce integrity, and says detectors may be used.

units.why: The letter says "Faculty members have complete discretion regarding the extent to which they will allow AI tools", the core delegation to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: Faculty members have complete discretion regarding the extent to which they will allow AI tools

units.why: The sentence lists a range from "(a) completely prohibiting" to "(c) allowing students to use all AI tools" with citation; this sorts options into named categories, matching P05 rather than P04, which covers who decides.
units.anchor: (a) completely prohibiting the use of AI tools, (b) asking that students consult with instructors
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P05; A gave modality informs, B may. The sentence lists the range 'completely prohibiting' to 'allowing students to use all AI tools' as options; it describes categories and grants nothing to anyone, so informs.

units.why: Option (c) expects that "students will properly cite their usage of such tools", a citation/disclosure expectation (P24) attached to open use.
units.anchor: students will properly cite their usage of such tools
units.resolution_why: Only B coded option (c), where students are expected to 'properly cite their usage of such tools'. The source states this citation expectation explicitly, so it is a real policy (P24) and is kept.

units.why: "Faculty should clearly communicate expectations regarding the use of AI tools to students in all course syllabi" tells instructors to put AI expectations in every syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: clearly communicate expectations regarding the use of AI tools to students in all course syllabi

units.why: "Faculty must enforce high ethical standards for students' academic conduct" requires instructors to enforce integrity rules; P36 (handled through integrity processes) is the closest.
units.anchor: Faculty must enforce high ethical standards for students’ academic conduct.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P36/must/instructor; A gave unit_stance restrict, B neutral. 'Faculty must enforce high ethical standards' is an enforcement duty with no AI limit of its own, so neutral.

units.why: "The university's various Academic Integrity policies prohibit academic dishonesty, including misrepresentation of a student's own work" says students' submissions must be their own (P29); AI is not named but the paragraph frames AI conduct.
units.anchor: prohibit academic dishonesty, including misrepresentation of a student’s own work
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P29; A coded general/informs/neutral, B during-work/must-not/prohibit. The source says the Academic Integrity policies 'prohibit academic dishonesty, including misrepresentation of a student's own work', a prohibition on students about what they submit, so must-not and prohibit; phase is during-work as it governs submitted work.

units.why: "Faculty may take advantage of software tools that can detect the use of AI by students" permits instructors to use detection software (P40), during misuse checks.
units.anchor: Faculty may take advantage of software tools that can detect the use of AI
units.frag_end: use of AI by students in their work.

units.why: The provost states that "students who use unapproved AI tools may be shortcutting the learning process to their ultimate disadvantage", a rationale that AI shortcuts skill-building practice (P41).
units.anchor: students who use unapproved AI tools may be shortcutting the learning process

units.why: The letter says "it is important for us to explore and to adapt to new technologies to better serve our students, since they will likely live in an increasingly technological world", giving a preparation-for-the-future rationale for engaging with AI (P44).
units.anchor: it is important for us to explore and to adapt to new technologies
units.frag_start: On the other hand, it is

units.why: "working with the Faculty Senate to form a committee to explore the broader implications of AI on teaching" announces a body to study AI and teaching going forward, so policy is expected to evolve (P54).
units.anchor: form a committee to explore the broader implications of AI on teaching
units.frag_end: charge and its membership are forthcoming.

units.why: The committee questions include "How will AI affect the ways that students learn", showing an intent to examine AI effects on learning; this is exploration of evidence (P55) rather than a rule.
units.anchor: How will AI affect the ways that students learn
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. The provost lists the committee's questions, including 'How will AI affect the ways that students learn', which signals the university will examine AI's effect on learning (P55). It is an informs unit, kept.

documents.unit: Office of the Provost (AI Task Force)
documents.title: Example AI Policies, Suitable for Course Syllabi
documents.stance_why: The page offers four sample syllabus texts from "No AI Usage Allowed" to "Unrestricted AI Usage" as "a starting point", so it is a set of tiers for instructors to choose from; it delegates.
tiers: Restricted AI Usage for Specific Tasks
documents.summary: The Provost's office offers four sample syllabus statements from full ban to unrestricted use, created by the AI Task Force. Faculty choose among them.

units.why: "Case Western Reserve University embraces AI in education to prepare students for the workforce" is a stated university position that teaching AI is a professional skill (P44) and welcomes AI.
units.anchor: embraces AI in education to prepare students for the workforce
units.frag_start: Case Western Reserve University embraces AI

units.why: "the university respects faculty's academic freedom to manage their classes" says course AI choices rest with faculty (P04).
units.anchor: the university respects faculty's academic freedom to manage their classes
units.frag_start: At the same time, the university

units.why: "This list of sample texts serves as a starting point for syllabi" introduces four named sample policies from permissive to restrictive, i.e. named categories of AI use (P05).
units.anchor: This list of sample texts serves as a starting point for syllabi
units.frag_end: consider how AI tools might be used.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P05/informs; A gave actor instructor, B admin. The page offers the samples to faculty to adapt for syllabi ('a starting point for syllabi'), so the instructor is addressed.

units.why: Template 1 states "Students are prohibited from using any AI tools... for any aspect of the course", a default ban on all course work (P01).
units.anchor: Students are prohibited from using any AI tools, algorithms, or technologies

units.why: "any violation of this policy may result in academic penalties" states consequences, but they are unspecified, so this is a penalty statement (P37) in weak form; it is not a concrete sanction.

units.frag_start: All work must be completed without

units.why: Sample 1 invites students to "consult with the instructor if they have any questions or concerns regarding the appropriate use of common/basic AI", i.e. ask when unsure (P10).
units.anchor: if they have any questions or concerns regarding the appropriate use of common/basic AI
units.frag_end: use of common/basic AI in this course.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P10; A gave phase during-work, B course-start. The sentence tells students to consult the instructor when unsure about use, which applies while they work, so during-work. Sentences repeating this in samples 2-4 are coded once.

units.why: Sample 2 says "Students are expected to use AI responsibly and critically evaluate the outputs of AI tools", requiring students to check AI output (P31).
units.anchor: critically evaluate the outputs of AI tools
units.frag_start: Students are expected to use AI

units.why: Sample 2: "Students can use basic AI tools for specific tasks approved by the instructor, such as grammar checking or citation formatting" allows only narrow, instructor-approved uses, mostly language tasks (P18).
units.anchor: Students can use basic AI tools for specific tasks approved by the instructor
units.frag_start: Students can use basic AI tools

units.why: "The use of AI should be justified based on its relevance to the learning objectives" sets a condition that AI use be justified by learning goals. No type covers a justification requirement.
units.anchor: The use of AI should be justified based on its relevance to the learning objectives
units.frag_start: The use of AI should be
units.uncovered_note: AI use must be justified by its relevance to the course learning objectives.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. 'The use of AI should be justified based on its relevance to the learning objectives' is a distinct rule from the understanding requirement in the same sentence. No existing type covers a justification requirement, so it stays UNCOVERED.

units.why: "students must demonstrate a clear understanding of both the AI methods employed and their academic application" requires understanding of what AI was used for (P30).
units.anchor: students must demonstrate a clear understanding of both the AI methods employed
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P30/must; A gave unit_stance require, B restrict. The sentence is a condition on AI use in the Restricted sample, not a requirement to use AI, so restrict.

units.why: Sample 3: "AI tools and methodologies are encouraged to enhance learning outcomes, improve efficiency, and explore innovative coursework approaches" welcomes AI by default (P02).
units.anchor: AI tools and methodologies are encouraged to enhance learning outcomes

units.why: "Guidelines for AI usage will be provided to ensure alignment with course objectives and academic standards" commits the instructor to give guidance (P09).
units.anchor: Guidelines for AI usage will be provided to ensure alignment with course objectives
units.frag_start: Guidelines for AI usage will be
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P09; A gave modality must, B informs. 'Guidelines for AI usage will be provided' commits the instructor to supply guidance, so must.

units.why: Sample 4: "Students have full autonomy to utilize AI technologies for all aspects of the course, including assignments, projects, research, and examinations" allows AI everywhere including exams, so it is a permit/encourage default (P02), not P22.
units.anchor: Students have full autonomy to utilize AI technologies for all aspects of the course
units.frag_start: Students have full autonomy to utilize
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P02/may; A gave unit_stance permit, B encourage. 'Students have full autonomy to utilize AI' grants permission and does not urge use (the next sentence does), so permit.

units.why: "students are encouraged to explore the full potential of AI in their academic pursuits" explicitly encourages use (P02).
units.anchor: students are encouraged to explore the full potential of AI
units.frag_start: There are no limitations on the
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. 'students are encouraged to explore the full potential of AI' is a separate encouraging sentence in the Unrestricted sample (P02), distinct from the autonomy sentence, so it is kept. A's A10 (a variant of the consult-the-instructor sentence repeated in sample 2) was dropped as an in-document repeat.

documents.unit: University Center for Innovation in Teaching and Education (UCITE)
documents.title: Teaching and Learning with Generative Artificial Intelligence Systems
documents.stance_why: The teaching center page advises faculty how to set and communicate their own policies ("Create, or co-create with students, appropriate policies") and sets no student rule of its own; it delegates.
documents.summary: The teaching center page advises faculty to learn about GenAI, talk openly with students, set course policies, and remind them of integrity rules and data privacy. It points to workshops, a Canvas course and a collection of syllabus statements.

units.why: The resource list item "AI Detection Services: Use with Caution" advises caution with detectors; P39 is the closest type though it does not say they are unreliable.
units.anchor: AI Detection Services: Use with Caution
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P39; A gave modality informs, B should. 'AI Detection Services: Use with Caution' advises caution, a recommendation to instructors, so should.

units.why: "AI can assist us as a thinking companion to improve our own decision-making" is a quoted view that AI supports rather than replaces human choices (P32).
units.anchor: AI can assist us as a thinking companion to improve our own decision-making
units.frag_start: AI can assist us as a
units.frag_end: relying on the AI to make choices for us)
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. The page quotes Mollick: 'AI can assist us as a thinking companion to improve our own decision-making ... (rather than simply relying on the AI to make choices for us)'. It is offered as guidance on how AI should serve thinking, matching P32; informs. Kept.

units.why: UCITE says faculty "can and should take time to reflect how, when, and where we improve student learning" with GenAI before deciding, i.e. faculty learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: faculty can and should take time to reflect how, when, and where
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P63/should; A gave unit_stance encourage, B neutral. The advice that faculty 'can and should take time to reflect' sets no stance on AI use itself, so neutral.

units.why: "UCITE can work with faculty to consider how course learning objectives or goals align with student assessments" offers consultation support (P63).
units.anchor: UCITE can work with faculty to consider how course learning objectives
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P63; A gave actor instructor, B admin. 'UCITE can work with faculty' is an offer by the teaching center, so admin.

units.why: The page describes a Canvas course titled "Getting Started with Generative AI in Education" for faculty and staff, which is faculty training (P63).
units.anchor: launched a Canvas course for faculty and staff members titled

units.why: "Take some time to experience and experiment with GenAI tools, like CWRU AI, Microsoft CoPilot, and ChatGPT" advises faculty to try tools before setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: Take some time to experience and experiment with GenAI tools

units.why: "Consumer AI services, especially free ones, often collect the data you enter into them and use that data in their training models" warns about data collection (P50).
units.anchor: Consumer AI services, especially free ones, often collect the data you enter
units.frag_end: made available via these AI services.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. 'Consumer AI services, especially free ones, often collect the data you enter into them' is a stated privacy fact supporting the data-protection advice (P50); informs. Kept.

units.why: "Never put sensitive university information into an AI service if the university does not have a contract" bans sensitive data in unvetted services (P50).
units.anchor: Never put sensitive university information into an AI service
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P50/must-not; A gave unit_stance prohibit, B restrict. 'Never put sensitive university information into an AI service' is a flat ban for that data, so prohibit.

units.why: "have open and transparent conversations with students about your expectations regarding ChatGPT or other GenAI tools" tells instructors to communicate expectations (P09).
units.anchor: have open and transparent conversations with students about your expectations
units.frag_start: To start, have open and transparent
units.frag_end: use of those systems in our courses.

units.why: "try not to rush to an assumption that students are necessarily going to cheat using GenAI tools" asks instructors to presume good faith; no type covers this stance, P57 is about talking before escalation.
units.anchor: try not to rush to an assumption that students are necessarily going to cheat
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should not presume that students will cheat with GenAI (presumption of good faith).

'try not to rush to an assumption that students are necessarily going to cheat' concerns how to treat suspected misuse, so when-misuse. P57 (talk to the student before escalating) does not fit, so UNCOVERED stands.
